{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-az-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"3f25d495fb72dfa13f1c0ebc1fa2bebb56b85b55c023c7432b3a1606acfd51ac","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-az-class-d:lineage:131","source_registry_sha256":"6dbbc2d22fea619728bdb90038a4aedf3afc07eab652b3f97027c9c69aaadaf4","source_liveness_sha256":"1c5753487760cbe2044d84b5696121c7181af61815b598d89d5ce158abf5fe43"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Remaining required equipment and the start of safe driving practices","heading":"C — Head restraints, muffler, emissions, windshield, mirrors, horn and lights; defensive driving, attitude, foresight, practice, distractions and the wireless-device law, steering and scanning","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Head restraints, muffler, emissions, windshield, mirrors, horn and lights; defensive driving, attitude, foresight, practice, distractions and the wireless-device law, steering and scanning
Knowledge domain: the last items of required vehicle equipment, then the opening of the safe driving practices chapter: what defensive driving means, the attitudes that keep you safe, how beginners and experienced drivers improve, the Arizona rules on phones and other wireless devices, and how to steer and scan.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Any child younger than 8 riding in a vehicle in Arizona has to be properly secured in a child passenger restraint system. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Head restraints on seat backs exist to lower the risk of a whiplash injury when you are hit from behind. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
An adjustable head restraint should sit against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
Every motor vehicle needs a muffler that works well and runs at all times, so it does not cause excessive pollution or unusual noise. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Fitting a muffler cut-out, a bypass or any similar device is illegal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
Motor vehicles of the 1967 model year or newer must have an exhaust emissions system to help cut air pollution. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
The engine of every motor vehicle must be equipped so that excessive fumes and smoke cannot escape. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A01
A vehicle must have a windshield with no cracks, and its windshield wipers must work properly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A01
Tint film on windows and windshields is legal only within certain limits, so owners should confirm the maker or installer follows Arizona law. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A01
If a vehicle's build or load blocks the driver's rear view, it needs at least one outside mirror on the driver side showing at least 200 feet of highway behind. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A01
Your vehicle must have a working horn that can be heard from 200 feet away. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A01
Emergency vehicles are the ones that may carry a siren, whistle or bell. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A01
Flashing red lights on the front of a vehicle are banned, even on a disabled vehicle, except on authorized emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A01
Turn on your hazard warning lights whenever your vehicle is stopped on the roadway or on the shoulder. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A01
Driving defensively protects both your life and your driving record, and it starts with constant awareness of conditions and planning ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
Defensive driving also means anticipating dangers and acting in time so that you never strike an obstacle or another vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
Even a crash with no injuries brings inconvenience and repair bills, and it can lead to a court appearance, fines and higher insurance rates. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A02
The manual names courtesy and consideration for others as the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A02
Concentration and alertness also matter, so make keeping your mind on the road a habit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A02
Driving while drowsy or emotionally upset can be as dangerous as driving impaired. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A02
Foresight is the ability to size up a traffic situation quickly and be ready to take corrective action. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A02
However many years you have driven, you will eventually meet equipment failures, bad weather, unskilled drivers and drivers who ignore the rules, and defensive driving is the best preparation. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A02
The defensive habits the manual lists are keeping good vision ahead and around you, staying alert, obeying speed limits and knowing when to slow or stop, and always wearing your safety belt. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A02
A defensive driver keeps looking ahead and around, checks the mirrors constantly, and watches for hazards in front, at the sides and behind. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A02
A beginner learns by instruction, observation and practice, and someone not in a driver training program should ask an experienced, skilled, licensed driver to help. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A02
Once you hold an instruction permit, practice starting, pulling out of a parking space, stopping and controlling the vehicle in a parking lot or other open area with little traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A03
Experienced drivers often struggle with carelessness, overconfidence and bad habits that build up over time. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A03
Driving rules and techniques have changed and traffic keeps growing, so how well you adapt decides how safe a driver you really are. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A03
The manual defines a driving skill as a rehearsed strategy of anticipating, reacting and constantly adjusting the space between you and other vehicles. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A03
Progress as a driver shows in dropping risk-taking, keeping to speed limits and being able to take corrective action when needed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A03
Distractions to avoid at the wheel include reading a GPS or map, using a phone or texting, hunting for a dropped item, tending to children and buckling a safety belt. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A03
If you need to use a cell phone or send or read a text, first pull safely off the road and stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A03
While you drive, both hands should be on the steering wheel so you keep full control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A03
Arizona law forbids holding or supporting a wireless device while driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A03
While driving you may not write or read any text-based message, and you may not watch, record or broadcast video. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A03
While driving, a driver may use a wireless device only to report an emergency or for hands-free or voice-to-text operation [A03].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A03
Hands-free and voice-to-text use of a wireless device is permitted. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A03
To stay in your lane, look well down the road and make only small steering corrections when needed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A03
Drivers tend to steer toward where they look, so in a curve or turn, looking toward the outside of your lane helps you stay in it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A03
Scan for cars, motorcycles, bicyclists, people and animals that may cross your path, especially at intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, construction areas and playgrounds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0024]

Misconceptions: the horn and rear-mirror distances are not two different numbers, both are the same distance; hazard flashers are for a stopped vehicle, while flashing red lights on the front are banned for ordinary vehicles even when disabled; a quick text is not an exception, since the only use the manual allows while driving is reporting an emergency, and anything else means pulling off and stopping first; buckling up is a distraction if you do it while moving, so fasten the belt before you start.
Mnemonics: Hold nothing, hands on the wheel — talk hands-free or stop; in a curve, eyes to the outside edge.
Glossary: whiplash means a neck injury from the head snapping back and forth, usually in a rear-end crash; muffler cut-out means a device that lets exhaust skip the muffler; foresight means sizing up traffic early enough to act; voice-to-text means dictating a message without touching the device.
Dynamic facts: the legal window-tint limits are not printed in the manual and must come from Arizona law, and the wireless-device rules are set by statute that can be amended, so confirm current wording on azdot.gov before teaching any detail beyond these pages.
